title: Safer links, better insight
intent: Stop short links from sending people to internal or operator-denied destinations, for new and existing links alike, and add an aggregate device breakdown to link statistics. No data that identifies a visitor is stored, as confirmed by the requester.

functionalRequirements.statement: A link cannot be created to an internal destination.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: A destination on a loopback, private, link-local or carrier-NAT address is rejected with 400, in IPv4 and IPv6 and in any numeric notation.
A destination named localhost, a single-label host name, or a name under an internal suffix is rejected with 400.

functionalRequirements.statement: The operator can deny destination hosts.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: A destination on a denied host, or any subdomain of one, is rejected with 400.
A malformed denylist stops the service at startup.

functionalRequirements.statement: The destination rules are enforced when a link is followed, so they also cover links that already exist.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: An existing link whose host is added to the denylist stops redirecting: 410 with code link_blocked and no Location header.
A blocked request records no click, and the response does not reveal the destination.
A stored link that points at an internal address is blocked the same way.

functionalRequirements.statement: Link statistics include a breakdown of clicks by device class.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: Each click is classified as desktop, mobile, tablet, bot or unknown from the request's User-Agent header.
Statistics report the number of clicks for every device class, in a fixed order.
Only the device class is stored. The User-Agent header is never stored.
Clicks recorded before this change are reported as unknown.

nonFunctionalRequirements.statement: No data that identifies a visitor is stored or logged: no client address, no User-Agent header, no visitor identifier.
Existing response fields keep their meaning; additions only.
The checks added to the redirect path need no network call and no additional database query.

ambiguities.question: Does marketing need to know about individual visitors (identity, repeat visits, location), or about the audience in aggregate (what kinds of devices, where the traffic comes from)?
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Identifying visitors means storing personal data such as IP addresses or persistent identifiers. That is a different data model, a privacy review, and it is costly to undo once the data has been collected. Aggregate figures need none of that.
options: Aggregate only: no data that identifies a visitor
Per-visitor: unique and returning visitors, which needs a stored identifier
Per-visitor with location, which needs the client address
ambiguities.defaultAssumption: Aggregate only. Nothing that identifies a visitor is stored.
ambiguities.resolution: Aggregate only. We must not store anything that identifies a visitor: no IP addresses, no raw user agents, no visitor IDs.

ambiguities.question: Which additional figures would count as better? Today a link reports total clicks, clicks per day and top referrers.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: It sets the scope of the analytics work and what must be stored per click.
options: Breakdown by browser and operating system
Conversion tracking on the destination site
ambiguities.defaultAssumption: Add a breakdown by device type (desktop, mobile, tablet, bot, unknown). It is the smallest addition that says something about the audience and needs no personal data.

ambiguities.question: Safer against what? Links that lead visitors to malicious or internal destinations, abuse of the API to create links in bulk, or people guessing or scraping other users' links?
ambiguities.whyItMatters: These are three unrelated pieces of work: destination rules, authentication and quotas, or code entropy and access control. Building the wrong one leaves the reported problem in place.
options: Unsafe destinations: block malicious and internal targets
API abuse: authentication and stricter limits
Link privacy: harder-to-guess codes, access control on stats
ambiguities.defaultAssumption: Unsafe destinations, because an open redirector's main risk is where it sends people.
ambiguities.resolution: Unsafe destinations. The concern is links that send people to malicious sites or to internal addresses. API abuse is a separate project.

ambiguities.question: How much is "something", and is there a date? Is a first slice of each ask acceptable?
ambiguities.whyItMatters: It decides whether to build the smallest useful version or wait for a complete one.
options: Smallest useful slice in the next release
ambiguities.defaultAssumption: The smallest slice that delivers both asks, in the next release, with the rest recorded as follow-ups.

ambiguities.question: Do new safety rules apply only to links created from now on, or also to links that already exist?
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Applying rules to existing links means checking at redirect time and can stop links that work today. Not applying them leaves every existing unsafe link live.
options: Existing links too, enforced when they are followed
ambiguities.resolution: Existing links too. If a destination is denied later, the old link must stop redirecting.

assumptions.statement: A denylist maintained by the operator is an acceptable first measure against malicious destinations.
Device classification from the User-Agent header is a heuristic and is good enough for audience reporting.

outOfScope: Identifying visitors, counting unique or returning visitors, and location
Authentication, quotas and other protection of the API itself
Checking destinations against a reputation service, and resolving host names to check the addresses they point to
Browser, operating system and hourly breakdowns
